name: setpriority
synopsis: int setpriority(int which, id_t who, int prio);
description: The setpriority() system call sets the scheduling priority (nice value) of a process, process group, or user as specified by the parameters. It adjusts the priority to influence CPU scheduling, with values clamped between -20 (highest) and 19 (lowest).

parameters.name: which
parameters.description: Specifies the type of entity to set priority for: PRIO_PROCESS, PRIO_PGRP, or PRIO_USER

parameters.name: who
parameters.description: The identifier for the entity, interpreted relative to 'which' (e.g., process ID, process group ID, or user ID)

parameters.name: prio
parameters.description: The new priority value, ranging from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest priority)

return_value.failure: Returns -1 on error, and sets errno to indicate the error

errors.description: The caller attempted to set a higher priority (lower nice value) without the required capability (CAP_SYS_NICE)
The 'which' argument is not one of the valid values (PRIO_PROCESS, PRIO_PGRP, or PRIO_USER)
A process was located, but the effective user ID does not match and the caller lacks the required capability
No process could be located using the given 'which' and 'who' values

bugs: Under Linux with NPTL, the nice value is treated as a per-thread attribute instead of per-process as required by POSIX, which may lead to non-portable behavior.
versions: POSIX.1-2001, SVr4, 4.4BSD; Linux 2.6.12 and later for certain privilege behaviors
